mappings.note: MISFILED natural-resources run continues. Tehri Dam and its river -- duplicate of qid:104734, mapped to the same earth-systems competency C 2.8.
The water-harvesting technique popular in Kerala (surangams) -- C 2.8, the hydrosphere strand.
Which is NOT a cause of water scarcity -- water availability within earth systems, C 2.8.
Which resource is inexhaustible -- classifying natural resources, C 2.8.

The role of forests -- their function in the ecosystem (habitat, water cycle, soil). Community and ecosystem level, so C 4.3 rather than the resource-classification C 2.8 used for the fuel and water items.
Which resource is exhaustible -- the complement of qid:104760, same code C 2.8.
How environmental quality can be improved -- resource use and pollution within earth systems, C 2.8.
The khadin system belongs to Rajasthan -- a water-harvesting structure, C 2.8.
Petroleum as an exhaustible fossil fuel -- resource classification, C 2.8.
The Sardar Sarovar Dam is on the Narmada -- large dams and water management, C 2.8.
When the Ganga Action Plan started -- river pollution control, C 2.8, as for qid:104736.
Who led the Arabari project (A. K. Banerjee). A named person in a conservation case study, so C 5.2 (Science in human life through Social Sciences and Ethics) rather than the ecological C 4.3.
Where most petroleum is consumed -- fossil-fuel use within earth systems, C 2.8.
Where the Arabari project began -- the same people-and-forests case study as qid:104768, C 5.2.
What national parks preserve -- protecting habitats and the species in them, an ecosystem-level idea, C 4.3.
The new approach to conservation is involving local communities as stakeholders. That is the social and ethical dimension, C 5.2, not the ecological content of C 4.3.
The tree Amrita Devi Bishnoi is associated with (khejri) -- the same named case study as qid:104732, and mapped identically.
What threatens genetic diversity in crops -- monoculture narrowing a population's variation, an ecosystem/population-level idea, C 4.3.
The three R's -- third occurrence of this item; mapped to C 2.8 like qid:104731 and qid:104753.
What reduces species diversity in the tropics -- habitat loss at the ecosystem level, C 4.3.
What wildlife conservation protects -- species and their habitats, C 4.3.
Which high-altitude plants have disappeared -- loss of species from a biome, C 4.3.
What is not permitted in a wildlife sanctuary -- how a protected ecosystem is managed, C 4.3.
LPG as domestic cooking gas -- a fossil-fuel product, C 2.8.
Which is NOT a fossil-fuel product -- energy-resource classification, C 2.8.

The free-living nitrogen-fixing bacterium (Azotobacter). Nitrogen fixation is an interaction that moves an element between organisms and their environment, which is C 4.3; C 3.2-LO-1 was considered but the question is about the bacterium, not about how a plant feeds.
Which are renewable energy sources -- resource classification, C 2.8.
What khadins are used for in Rajasthan -- water harvesting, C 2.8, matching qid:104764.
Which is NOT a natural resource -- resource classification, C 2.8.
Which term refers to plants and animals (the biotic component / flora and fauna) -- a level-of-organisation term in an ecosystem, C 4.3. Last of the misfiled natural-resources run.

The green pigment absorbing light is chlorophyll. The question asks for the pigment inside the chloroplast, so C 3.1 (cellular components) rather than C 3.2-LO-1, which is reserved here for the process of autotrophic nutrition.
Raw materials, conditions, products and equation of photosynthesis -- the full statement of autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Assertion-reason: plants make their own food because chlorophyll absorbs light. The reasoning links chlorophyll to autotrophy, which is the autotrophic clause of C 3.2-LO-1.
True/false: oxygen is a product of photosynthesis -- C 3.2-LO-1.

The pores through which a leaf exchanges gases are stomata. Naming the route of gas exchange in a plant is the exchange-of-materials strand of C 3.2; C 3.1 is reserved for questions about the guard cell's own mechanism.
Describe an experiment proving CO2 is necessary for photosynthesis. Content is autotrophic nutrition (C 3.2-LO-1); designing the KOH control and predicting the starch-test result is C 8.1.

Most absorption happens in the small intestine. Names the organ only, so the nutrition-sequence outcome C 3.2-LO-1, not the villus structure-function outcome -- the same distinction drawn for qid:104690.
Trace food through the alimentary canal, naming what happens at each stage -- the steps of nutrition in human beings, C 3.2-LO-1.
Labelled digestive-system diagram marking where each kind of digestion occurs -- C 3.2-LO-1.
The human heart has four chambers -- an organ of the transport pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
Path of blood through the heart, naming chambers and vessels in order -- C 3.2-LO-2.
The left ventricle has the thickest wall -- heart structure within human transport, C 3.2-LO-2.

Beats per hour from 72 per minute. The physiology is the human heart (C 3.2-LO-2); turning a rate into a total is the mathematical-model clause of C 8.1, which is what makes this item different from the recall questions beside it.
The kidney's basic filtration unit is the nephron -- named in C 4.2-LO-1, and 'filtration unit' is a structure-to-function phrasing.
Why a healthy person's urine has no glucose -- selective reabsorption in the tubule. The excretory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
Assertion-reason: urine is not simply the glomerular filtrate, although the glomerulus does filter under pressure. Tests the reabsorption step of the human excretory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
The artificial blood-filtering process is dialysis -- the human excretory pathway and its clinical substitute, C 3.2-LO-2.
Explain urine formation and evaluate why dialysis cannot fully replace a kidney. Both halves are the human excretory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
From 180 litres filtered and 1.8 litres passed, compute the percentage reabsorbed and comment. Excretion physiology (C 3.2-LO-2) plus a quantitative model of it (C 8.1).
Gas exchange happens across the alveolar wall -- C 4.2-LO-1 names the alveolus.
How the lungs are adapted to maximise gas exchange -- alveolar surface area and thin walls, C 4.2-LO-1.
Assertion-reason: the alveolar wall is one cell thick, which shortens the diffusion distance. This is the structure-to-function link C 4.2-LO-1 asks for, stated exactly.
Air breathed in an hour from 16 breaths a minute at 500 mL. Respiratory physiology (C 3.2-LO-2) with a quantitative computation (C 8.1), matching how qid:707060 is treated.

Draw and label the respiratory system, then annotate the adaptations for gas exchange. The labelling is the pathway and its organs (C 3.2-LO-2); the annotation is alveolar structure serving function (C 4.2-LO-1).
The end product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle is lactic acid -- products of respiration, C 3.2-LO-3.
Why aerobic respiration yields far more energy from the same glucose -- complete vs partial oxidation. The energy clause of C 3.2-LO-3.
Assertion-reason: anaerobic respiration is NOT more efficient although it needs no oxygen. Turns on comparative energy yield, C 3.2-LO-3.
Double circulation means blood passes twice through the heart per cycle -- C 3.2-LO-2.
Why birds and mammals need double circulation but fishes do not -- high metabolic rate and the need to keep blood unmixed. Human/animal transport pathway, C 3.2-LO-2.
Water rises in a tall tree chiefly by transpiration pull -- xylem transport, C 4.3-LO-1.
